author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Three Unsigned Letters
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
The three letters arrived in an envelope that had been opened before it reached us.

There was no attempt to hide it. The seal had been cut cleanly, and the flap was folded back with the tidy care of somebody who believed procedure excused curiosity.

Severus held it beneath the archive lamp.

"I see," he said.

I had learned that those two words could mean anything from mild irritation to the beginning of a personal storm.

"What is it?"

"The committee."

He showed me the attached receipt. The Lanternweald Historical Committee had accepted a packet of wartime correspondence for review, then forwarded three items it considered relevant to Professor Severus Snape. The note asked him to identify the writers, confirm which were authentic, and authorize public display before the upcoming Closed Bells exhibit.

"Did they ask you whether they could open the packet?" I said.

"No."

"Did the sender?"

"The sender requested the letters be delivered to me. Not to the committee."

I looked at the paper again.

The request was written in small print beneath a list of accession numbers, as though permission were a box that could be ticked by someone who had never been afraid of an envelope.

"What do you want to do?" I asked.

He placed the letters on the table without opening them.

"At present? Break something."

"Anything in particular?"

"The assumption that an archive is entitled to the contents of every grief it can find."

I wanted to make a joke about how expensive that assumption would be to break, but the expression on his face stopped me.

Neri came to the workroom when I sent for them. They listened while Severus explained what had happened. Their cheeks reddened.

"The committee meant to preserve the chain of custody," they said.

"Then perhaps," Severus replied, "they should have preserved the seals."

Neri flinched.

I watched them closely. The Closed Bells history had already shown how people could turn safety into control when they grew frightened. Here was a quieter version: a group deciding that historical importance outranked the person whose name was on a letter.

"What is the actual rule?" I asked.

Neri sighed.

"There is no written rule about personal mail in the archives."

"Then this is where we write one."

Severus glanced at me. He did not look grateful yet.

He looked tired.

We brought the committee chair to the archive after lunch. They were a brisk person named Vale, with ink-stained fingers and a habit of consulting a notebook while others spoke.

"The letters concern a war," Vale said. "They could be historically significant."

"So could my grocery lists," Severus replied. "Would you like to display those too?"

Vale looked at me for help.

I did not give it.

"Whether something matters to history isn't the same question as whether you have permission to open it," I said. "The sender's instructions were clear."

"We were afraid the packet might contain an active threat."

"Then you should have used an agreed safety process and documented it," Neri said. "Not turned a private letter into reading material for the entire committee."

Vale's face tightened.

"That wasn't our intention."

"Then we need a process that doesn't depend on intention," I answered.

Severus was silent for a long time. I could see him weighing whether the discussion was worth participating in at all.

At last he said, "Return the original seals, document who opened the packet, and withdraw the request for public display. I will decide whether to read the letters. That is not a decision I will outsource."

Vale looked as if they wanted to object.

Neri spoke first.

"Agreed."

It took another hour to write the incident report. No one enjoyed it. That was probably a sign that we were finally doing the work.

After the committee left, Severus took the letters to the small room above the archive. It was a place with one window, two chairs, and a table too narrow for comfort. He had once called it an architectural error. Today he asked me to sit there with him.

"Do you want me to stay while you read them?"

"I want you here. I may not want to speak."

"That works."

He opened the first letter.

His expression did not change much. His thumb pressed harder against the paper.

He read the second, then placed it face down.

For a while he left the third unopened.

I watched the light crawl across the window frame. From the square below came the faint noise of market carts and a distant argument about cabbages.

"Do you want me to make tea?" I asked.

"Not yet."

I waited.

Eventually Severus spoke.

"The first is from someone who mistook obedience for loyalty. The second is from someone who knew better and was too frightened to act."

I did not ask which people.

"And the third?" I said.

He touched the sealed edge.

"I don't know."

"You're allowed not to open it today."

His eyes moved to mine.

"That is an irritatingly simple statement."

"One of my gifts."

He looked down at the paper again.

"For years I believed that every mistake had to be accounted for at once. If I delayed, I was shirking a duty. If I spoke, someone might use the words against me. There was no correct move."

"And now?"

"Now I am unsure whether that was duty or the shape fear took when I called it discipline."

I didn't have a clever answer. Sometimes the most loving thing I could do was not invent one.

I took his hand where it rested beside the unopened letter.

"You can choose tomorrow," I said. "Or never. If there's a genuine danger to other people, we handle that. But you don't owe anyone your private thoughts as a public exhibit."

He breathed in, slowly.

"Will you ask me about the contents later?"

"Only if you invite me."

He studied me.

"How do you manage to be both relentlessly curious and intolerably restrained?"

"I contain multitudes."

"An unfortunate number."

I smiled.

He did not quite smile back, but his hand tightened around mine.

We left the third letter sealed. He wrote a short note to the sender thanking them for trusting him with the packet, and he asked Neri to return the committee's original receipt with a correction. The letters would remain private unless Severus chose otherwise.

That evening we walked to Spinner's End through the Moonroot Door. The house smelled of rain and old wood. He took off his coat, hung it neatly, and stopped in the hallway.

"I was afraid," he said.

"Today?"

"That you would think I was hiding something from you."

I turned toward him.

"You are allowed to have things that belong to you."

"Even if you love me?"

"Especially then."

He reached for my hand again. His fingers were cool from the walk. When he lifted them to his mouth, the kiss was brief and oddly reverent.

"Stay?" he asked.

"I'd like to."

He nodded, and something in his expression eased.

We made tea. We did not talk about the letters over dinner. Later, when he kissed me beside the kitchen door, the familiar sharpness in his manner had gone quiet enough for me to notice how carefully he was listening for my answer.

"Yes," I whispered before he asked.

He smiled against my cheek.

The lamps burned low. The rest of the evening remained ours.

The next morning, the sealed letter lay exactly where he had left it.

Some things were not meant to be opened merely because someone had found the key.
